title: How do businesses make money, and why does it matter in a case?
description: The common ways companies earn money, from selling products to subscriptions, marketplaces and advertising, and what each means for a case.
hook: Businesses make money in a handful of recurring ways (selling products, selling people's time, subscriptions, marketplaces, advertising, freemium, razor and blades, and licensing or franchising), and each one has its own revenue formula and its own few numbers that matter. In a case, asking "how does this business make money?" early tells you which numbers to request, where problems usually hide and which ideas will actually work. Many candidates skip the question because it feels basic; it is one of the most useful you can ask.

Why the business model comes first

A generic "revenue and costs" structure works for any company, which is exactly its weakness: it does not show the interviewer that you understand this one. Once you know the model, you can split revenue into the pieces that actually move. A falling subscription business needs you to look at new customers, cancellations and price. A falling marketplace needs you to look at both sides of the market and the platform's cut. Asking about the model in your clarifying questions costs ten seconds and makes everything after it sharper.

The eight models you will meet most often

1. Selling products

Make or buy something and sell it for more than it cost: a bakery, a car maker, a clothing shop. Profit = volume × (price − cost per unit) − fixed costs. In a case, look at units sold, price and cost per unit, and how much of the cost base is fixed (see operating leverage).

2. Selling services by the hour or project

Law firms, agencies, builders and consultancies sell people's time. Revenue = billable staff × available hours × utilisation × realised rate. Utilisation, the share of paid time spent on work clients pay for, is the key number, because salaries are fixed. Suppose 50 consultants each have 1,800 workable hours a year, bill 70% of them and realise $150 an hour: revenue is 50 × 1,800 × 70% × $150 = $9.45M. Lifting utilisation to 75% with the same people and rates gives $10.125M, an extra $675k, if the work is there.

3. Subscriptions

Customers pay every month or year: streaming, software, gyms, phone contracts. What matters is how many join, what each pays and how long they stay. A small change in churn has a big effect over time. If 5% leave each month, the average customer stays about 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20 months; cut churn to 2.5% and they stay about 40 months, doubling what each customer is worth. The SaaS cases article goes deeper.

4. Marketplaces and platforms

Ride-hailing, food delivery and online marketplaces connect buyers and sellers and take a cut of the value of transactions, called the take rate. Revenue = value of transactions × take rate. A freelance marketplace handling $200M of jobs a year at a 10% take rate earns $20M. Both sides matter: riders want lots of drivers, drivers want lots of riders, so these businesses often spend heavily early to grow both. See network effects and platforms.

5. Advertising

The user pays nothing; advertisers pay to reach them. Search engines, social networks and free news sites work this way. Revenue = users × ads seen per user × price per ad, usually quoted per thousand views (CPM). An app with 2M daily users who each see 30 ads a day serves 60M ads a day. At a $5 CPM that is $300k a day, about $110M a year. In a case, anything that reduces engagement reduces revenue, even though users never pay.

6. Freemium

A free version attracts many users and a small share pay for more. The critical numbers are the conversion rate from free to paid and the cost of serving free users. With 1M free users, 4% converting at $10 a month brings 40,000 × $120 = $4.8M a year. If each free user costs $0.20 a month to serve, that is $2.4M, leaving $2.4M. If conversion slips to 3%, paid revenue is $3.6M and the margin over free-user costs halves to $1.2M.

7. Razor and blades

Sell the main product cheaply, then profit on the refills: printers and ink, coffee machines and pods, game consoles and games. Take a printer sold at $60 that costs $70 to make, a $10 loss. If the owner buys four $30 cartridges a year for three years, each costing $8 to make, the cartridges earn 12 × $22 = $264, so the customer is worth $254. Losing the refills to cheaper copies, or to customers printing less, is the serious threat.

8. Licensing and franchising

The company lets others use its brand, recipe or technology for a fee or a share of sales. Many fast-food chains are mostly franchised. The company earns less per outlet but takes far less risk and needs far less capital to grow (worked through in restaurant cases).

The models side by side

ModelRevenue driverNumber to ask for first
ProductsVolume × priceCost per unit, fixed costs
ServicesStaff × hours × utilisation × rateUtilisation
SubscriptionCustomers × price × lifetimeChurn
MarketplaceTransaction value × take rateSupply and demand on each side
AdvertisingUsers × ads seen × price per adEngagement
FreemiumFree users × conversion × priceConversion, cost of free users
Razor and bladesInstalled base × refill purchasesRefill rate and share
FranchisingOutlets × sales × royaltySales per outlet

Same revenue, very different businesses

Take three businesses that each report $10M of revenue. A supermarket sells low-margin goods often: revenue = customers × visits × average basket, and a 3% operating margin would be normal. A software company sells access to the same product again and again, at a high gross margin but with heavy upfront sales spend. A consultancy sells capacity, so idle staff destroy profit quickly. Equal revenue does not mean equal profit, risk or value. That is why the model, not the revenue figure, should shape your thinking.

How to use this in a case

Ask how the client makes money, then build your structure around the answer: for a subscription business, split revenue into new customers, retained customers and price; for a marketplace, look at both sides and the take rate; for a services firm, look at headcount, utilisation and rates.

Weak: "I'd look at revenue and costs. On revenue, price and volume."
Strong: "Since this is a subscription gym, I'd split revenue into new members, members who cancel and the monthly fee. If revenue fell while sign-ups held up, cancellations are where I'd start."

The strong answer is no longer than the weak one. It just shows that you have thought about this business.

Common mistakes

  • Skipping the question. It is not too basic. The answer decides your structure.
  • Forcing a product lens onto everything. "Price × volume" is awkward for a marketplace or an ad-funded app. Use the model's own formula.
  • Looking at one side of a platform. Falling orders on a delivery app may be a restaurant supply problem, not a customer problem.
  • Forgetting hybrid models. Many companies combine models, for example a gym with memberships plus personal training, or a streaming service with subscriptions plus ads. Ask what share of revenue each brings.

Practise

1. Write the revenue formula for a gym chain, a food delivery app and a law firm.

Show the answer

Gym: members × monthly fee (plus extras such as personal training), driven by joiners and churn. Delivery app: orders × average order value × commission rate, plus delivery fees paid by customers. Law firm: lawyers × available hours × utilisation × realised hourly rate.

2. An ad-funded app's daily users fall 10%, but time spent per user rises 5%, and ads per minute and ad prices are unchanged. What happens to revenue?

Show the answer

Revenue moves with users × time: 0.90 × 1.05 = 0.945, so revenue falls about 5.5%.

3. A printer company's profit has fallen even though it sells as many printers as before. What is your first hypothesis?

Show the answer

It is a razor-and-blades business, so profit sits in the cartridges. The likely cause is fewer cartridge sales per printer: customers printing less, or buying cheaper third-party cartridges. Ask for cartridge sales per installed printer over time.

Where to go next

Read unit economics to test whether one order, customer or store makes money. Then try the PrintWell case (razor and blades in trouble) and the Patchwork case (a marketplace changing its take rate). The industry articles apply these models to airlines, banks, hotels and more.
